---
title: "R → MapLibre Bridge"
subtitle: "Bringing data from an R cell to a reactive map"
---

## What this bridge is

As with [the Python bridge](bridge-python-maplibre.qmd): R **has no
idea MapLibre exists**. An R cell returns plain GeoJSON — a nested
list, or the equivalent of a converted `sf` object — as its last
expression; an `{ojs}` cell reads that value and draws it on the map.
No map-specific R function, however light: nothing to learn beyond R
itself.

::: {.callout-note}
**Historical note**: an earlier version of this page taught some
webgeods-specific R functions (`webgeods_map()` and similar) that
accumulated a queue of MapLibre commands to replay — because R
doesn't have (and never had) convenient access to Kyle Walker's real
`mapgl` library: `library(mapgl)` alone took **~120 seconds and
67MB** on first use in webR, because of heavy dependencies (`terra`,
`shiny`, `bslib`, `rmarkdown`) loaded regardless even if never used.
With the model described here, that problem no longer arises: R
doesn't need ANY map-specific function, it just returns GeoJSON — the
question "is it worth loading a package just for this" doesn't even
come up, because no package is needed.
:::

## The map on this page

It's created only once, when the page opens — same as in the Python
lesson.

<div id="bridge-map-r" style="height: 400px; width: 100%; border: 1px solid #5a4f3e;"></div>

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bridgeMapR = {
  const m = new WebGeoDS.Map("bridge-map-r", {
    center: [12.4964, 41.9028], // Rome
    zoom: 5,
    style: "https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/positron"
  });
  await m.ready();
  return m;
}
```

## The two parts of the bridge

### 1. The R cell — return GeoJSON, not a map object

```r
list(type = "FeatureCollection", features = list(
  list(type = "Feature", properties = list(name = "Rome"), geometry = list(type = "Point", coordinates = c(12.4964, 41.9028)))
))
```

A nested R list, the cell's last expression — no installation, no
`library()`. With an `sf` object, the conversion goes through
`geojsonsf`/`jsonlite`, already used elsewhere on this site:

```r
geojsonsf::sf_geojson(sf::st_transform(data, 4326)) |> jsonlite::fromJSON(simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

`sf_geojson()` doesn't reproject on its own (verified: with an `sf`
in EPSG:3857 it produces coordinates in meters, not degrees) —
`st_transform(data, 4326)` must be called explicitly first, exactly
like `.to_crs(4326)` on the Python side.

### 2. `getCellValue` + `setGeoJSON` — read and draw

Identical to the Python lesson — not by chance: it's the **exact
same** pair of functions, generic with respect to whichever language
produced the GeoJSON.

```js
value = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("my-cell-id", Generators)
{
  if (value) await myMap.setGeoJSON("my-source", value);
}
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Watch out for state**: as with Python, it isn't the R cell that
"remembers" what's on the map, it's the **source** — it stays as it
is until you update it with another `setGeoJSON()` on the same id, or
clear it.
:::

## Example 1 — a source with one point

```{.webgeods-r #bridge-cell-r1}
list(type = "FeatureCollection", features = list(
  list(type = "Feature", properties = list(name = "Rome"), geometry = list(type = "Point", coordinates = c(12.4964, 41.9028)))
))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bridgeCellR1 = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("bridge-cell-r1", Generators)
{
  if (bridgeCellR1) await bridgeMapR.setGeoJSON("bridge-points-r", bridgeCellR1);
}
```

## Example 2 — updating the same source with more points

Same `"bridge-points-r"` source as Example 1: it doesn't recreate it,
it updates it.

```{.webgeods-r #bridge-cell-r2}
list(type = "FeatureCollection", features = list(
  list(type = "Feature", properties = list(name = "Rome"), geometry = list(type = "Point", coordinates = c(12.4964, 41.9028))),
  list(type = "Feature", properties = list(name = "Milan"), geometry = list(type = "Point", coordinates = c(9.19, 45.4642)))
))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bridgeCellR2 = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("bridge-cell-r2", Generators)
{
  if (bridgeCellR2) await bridgeMapR.setGeoJSON("bridge-points-r", bridgeCellR2);
}
```

## Example 3 — restyling: a JS job, not an R one

As in the Python lesson: changing the color or radius isn't about
the data, so it's not R's concern. `{ojs}` decides it, directly on
the native MapLibre instance:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
restyleBridgePointsR = {
  const button = document.createElement("button");
  button.textContent = "Color the points terracotta";
  button.onclick = () => {
    bridgeMapR.map.setPaintProperty("bridge-points-r", "circle-color", "#b0522c");
    bridgeMapR.map.setPaintProperty("bridge-points-r", "circle-radius", 10);
  };
  return button;
}
```

${restyleBridgePointsR}

Same rule as the Python lesson: **R answers "what is this data", JS
decides "what should the user see of it"** — neither language knows
about the other beyond this boundary.

## Reference — the part of `map.js` relevant here

| Method | Effect |
|---|---|
| `setGeoJSON(sourceId, data, options)` | Creates the source/layer if it doesn't exist, otherwise just updates the data. `options.paint` sets the style ONLY at creation time. |
| `getGeoJSON(sourceId)` | Reads back the GeoJSON currently on the source. |
| `addMarkers(sourceId, options)` / `clearMarkers(sourceId)` | Markers on a subset of features (`options.filter`/`options.property`). |
| `highlight(sourceId, featureIds)` / `clearHighlights(sourceId)` | Highlights specific features on a dedicated layer, without touching the base style. |

For anything more specific than these, `sharedMap.map` is the native
MapLibre GL JS instance — no wrapper to work around.
